headline: House votes to make daylight saving time permanent

sources.title: House passes bill to make daylight saving time permanent
House passes bill to make daylight saving time permanent
House passes Trump-backed bill that would make daylight saving time permanent
House passes Sunshine Protection Act to make daylight saving time permanent (video, NBC Connecticut)

chunks.text: The US House of Representatives wants to {{do away with}} the twice-a-year clock changes. On Tuesday, [[lawmakers]] {{voted for}} a [[bill]] called the Sunshine Protection Act by 308 votes to 117. The plan would {{lock in}} [[permanent]] [[daylight saving time]] all across the country. Many [[supporters]] say the change is [[long overdue]].

verbs.wrong: To escape punishment for a bad action
verbs.why: A company might do away with an old rule that no longer makes sense, and a city might do away with a parking fee downtown. The House voted to do away with the twice a year clock change entirely.

verbs.correct: To officially support or choose something in a vote
verbs.wrong: To formally suggest a new law for others to study
verbs.why: Citizens vote for a candidate in an election, and city council members vote for a new budget each year. In this case, lawmakers voted for the Sunshine Protection Act by 308 votes to 117.

verbs.correct: To make something permanent so it cannot change
verbs.wrong: To close a place with a key so no one can leave
verbs.why: A buyer might lock in a low interest rate before it rises, and a shopper might lock in a sale price online. This bill would lock in permanent daylight saving time across the whole country.

chunks.text: So what does 'changing the clocks' [[actually]] mean? In many countries, people turn their clocks forward by one hour in spring and back again in fall. This [[custom]] is called daylight saving time, and it helps people {{make use of}} the extra evening light in summer. The original goal was also to save energy. But twice each year, millions of people must {{get used to}} a new [[schedule]], and [[the switch]] can {{throw off}} their sleep for several days.

verbs.correct: To use something that is available to you
verbs.wrong: To enjoy something in your free time
verbs.why: A student might make use of free time to read, and a family might make use of a park near their home. Daylight saving time helps people make use of the extra evening light in summer.

verbs.correct: To slowly become comfortable with something new
verbs.wrong: To learn how to do something difficult for the first time
verbs.why: New employees get used to a different schedule, and travelers get used to a new time zone after a few days. Twice each year, millions of Americans must get used to a new sleep schedule.

verbs.correct: To disturb or upset how something works
verbs.wrong: To make someone feel very tired
verbs.why: Jet lag can throw off a traveler's sleep for days, and a late train can throw off an entire morning schedule. The twice yearly clock change can throw off people's sleep for several days each time.

chunks.text: Many lawmakers were [[eager to]] {{press ahead}} with the plan, and the vote was [[bipartisan]]. They [[argue]] that lighter evenings could {{cut down on}} car accidents and give families more time outdoors after work. Several doctors add that a [[steady]] clock would be better for people. President Trump has {{come out}} [[in favor of]] the [[measure]] and has promised to sign it into law.

verbs.correct: To continue with a plan in a determined way
verbs.wrong: To hurry to finish something before a deadline
verbs.why: A city council might press ahead with a project despite complaints, and a company might press ahead with layoffs despite protest. Many lawmakers were eager to press ahead with this plan for permanent daylight time.

verbs.correct: To reduce the amount or number of something
verbs.why: A new stoplight can cut down on car accidents at a busy corner, and a diet can cut down on sugar over time. Supporters say lighter evenings under this bill could cut down on car accidents after work.

verbs.correct: To publicly say what you think or support
verbs.wrong: To make a public promise or guarantee
verbs.why: A senator might come out against a tax increase, and a mayor might come out in favor of a new park. President Trump has come out in favor of this bill and promised to sign it.

chunks.text: The bill now {{moves on}} to the [[Senate]], where its future is [[far from clear]]. Not every lawmaker {{goes along with}} the idea. [[Critics]] [[warn]] that winter mornings would stay dark for much longer, which could be risky for children who walk to school. Others recall that the country tried permanent daylight time back in 1973 but [[gave up on]] it [[within a year]]. For now, Americans must [[wait to see]] whether the Senate will {{take on}} the bill.

verbs.correct: To go forward to the next stage or step
verbs.wrong: To forget about the past and continue with life
verbs.why: A team moves on to the next round after a win, and a student moves on to the next chapter after a test. This bill now moves on to the Senate, where its future is far from certain.

verbs.correct: To agree with or accept an idea or plan
verbs.wrong: To pretend to agree while secretly disagreeing
verbs.why: A worker might go along with a manager's plan without full agreement, and a friend might go along with a group's decision to keep the peace. Not every lawmaker in Washington goes along with this idea.

verbs.correct: To accept and start handling a hard task
verbs.wrong: To politely refuse an offer of extra work
verbs.why: A new manager might take on more responsibility right away, and an employee might take on a difficult new project. For now, Americans must wait to see whether the Senate will take on this bill at all.

mainIdea.s: Most lawmakers in the House voted for a bill to lock in daylight saving time all year. The bill now goes to the Senate, which has not yet decided whether to pass it.
mainIdea.why: The House voted 308 to 117 to lock in permanent daylight saving time. The bill still needs Senate approval, and its future there is far from clear.

mainIdea.s: The bill has already become law after the Senate quickly agreed to the plan. Every lawmaker in Congress went along with the change, and no one raised any concern.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the bill only passed the House, so it is not law yet. It still needs the Senate, and the story says the outcome there is far from clear.

mainIdea.s: In the European Union, lawmakers have debated for years whether to end seasonal clock changes. So far, member states have not agreed on one time zone for the group.
mainIdea.why: This is about the European Union's separate, long debate over ending seasonal clock changes. It is a different country and a different bill from the US House vote.

tf.s: The House voted for the Sunshine Protection Act by 308 votes to 117.

tf.s: The bill would lock in permanent standard time and make winter evenings darker.
tf.why: The bill would lock in permanent daylight saving time, not standard time, so evenings would be lighter.

tf.s: President Trump has come out against the plan and refused to sign it.
tf.why: Trump has actually come out in favor of the measure and promised to sign it into law.

tf.s: The bill now moves on to the Senate, where its future is unclear.
tf.why: The story says the bill moves on to the Senate, where its future is far from clear.

tf.s: Permanent daylight saving time would do away with the twice-a-year clock changes.
tf.why: The plan would do away with the switch, so people would no longer change their clocks each spring and fall.

tf.s: The United States tried permanent daylight time in 1973, and the change lasted for many years before it ended.
tf.why: The story says the country tried permanent daylight time in 1973 but gave up on it within a year, not many years.

lines.text: The House just voted to {{do away with}} clock changes. Permanent daylight saving time, all year.
Wait, no more moving clocks twice a year? [[Finally]].
That's how a lot of people feel. Lawmakers {{voted for}} the Sunshine Protection Act, 308 to 117. It would {{lock in}} daylight time across the country.
Why do we even change the clocks?

The custom helps people {{make use of}} the extra evening light in summer, and it was supposed to save energy. But twice a year, millions have to {{get used to}} a new schedule, and the switch can {{throw off}} their sleep for days.
[[Tell me about it]]. [[I'm a zombie]] every spring.

Supporters were eager to {{press ahead}}. They say lighter evenings could {{cut down on}} car accidents and give families more time outside. President Trump has {{come out}} in favor and promised to sign it.
Not yet. The bill {{moves on}} to the Senate, and not everyone {{goes along with}} it. Critics warn winter mornings would stay dark much longer, which is risky for kids walking to school.
In 1973. The country quit within a year. We'll see if the Senate wants to {{take on}} the bill.
My sleep schedule and I will be watching closely.
